easy.q: Whose invitation got Elder Kyungu thinking about the words he uses?
options: President Oaks
President Monson
Elder Soares
easy.why: Elder Kyungu said he began pondering President Oaks’s invitation to use the language of peacemakers and how he could act on it with faith.

easy.q: Elder Kyungu’s talk was mostly about being careful with what?
options: The money we spend
The words we say
The food we eat
easy.why: He taught that “We must choose language that strengthens confidence and preserves relationships.” Our words can bring peace.

easy.q: Which of these is one of the peaceful things Elder Kyungu said we can say?
options: “Leave me alone.”
“Just stop talking.”
“Let us start again.”
easy.why: “Let us start again” was on his list of words that encourage understanding and peace. The other two were on his list of words to stop using.

easy.q: The converted Lamanites buried their weapons of war for peace. What did Elder Kyungu say we can bury?
options: Words that start fights
Things we no longer need
Memories that make us sad
easy.why: He said that like the Lamanites who “buried the weapons of war, for peace,” we can bury the language of contention for peace.

easy.q: Elder Kyungu said the Savior’s peace is real and powerful. Where did he say it begins?
options: With the leaders of countries
With other people being kind first
With us, in our hearts and words
easy.why: He said this peace “begins with us—with our hearts, our choices, and our words.” We do not have to wait for anyone else.

medium.q: Elder Kyungu said the prophet’s invitation to use the language of peacemakers is “not a simple suggestion.” What did he say it is?
options: A goal for the coming year
A reminder meant for leaders
A call to discipleship
A rule mainly for families
medium.why: Because the invitation comes from the living prophet, he called it “a call to discipleship as we follow Jesus Christ.”

medium.q: What “spiritual exercise” did Elder Kyungu describe?
options: Staying silent whenever we disagree with someone
Counting how many kind words we say each day
Listing the unkind things others have said to us
Finding words to give up and replacing them with peaceful ones
medium.why: He described identifying the language we need to forgo and then replacing it with “words and phrases that bring peace wherever we are and at all times.”

medium.q: According to Elder Kyungu, what do expressions like “You never listen” do?
options: Weaken love and damage relationships
Help others see their faults honestly
Do little harm when said in private
Hurt only when they come from strangers
medium.why: He taught that such words never edify: “They weaken love, diminish respect, and damage relationships.”

medium.q: Elder Kyungu quoted the New Testament: “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.” What does this show about our words?
options: We should say everything that we feel
What we say comes from what fills our hearts
A person’s way of speaking cannot be changed
Kind words matter more than what we feel
medium.why: Because speech flows from the heart, he went on to invite us to fill our hearts with the doctrine of Christ, which can change our language.

medium.q: Elder Kyungu asked us to pray for peaceful communication “regardless of the difference in our opinions.” What does that phrase teach?
options: We should keep our opinions to ourselves
Peace comes once everyone thinks alike
Differences are best settled by leaders
We can speak peacefully even when we disagree
medium.why: He did not ask us to agree on everything. He asked us to use language that “uplifts, edifies, comforts, and brings people together” even when opinions differ.

hard.q: Which situation best fits what Elder Kyungu taught about a tense disagreement?
options: Ana waits to speak kindly until her brother apologizes
Ana says, “Let us slow down and talk.”
Ana calmly explains that it is all his fault
Ana tells her brother to leave her alone for now
hard.why: “Let us slow down and talk” is among the words he offered in place of language that escalates “feelings of anger, disappointment, and frustration.”

hard.q: Elder Kyungu said that as we follow Jesus Christ we will do more than feel His peace. Quoting Elder Soares, what else did he say can happen?
options: We can become instruments of His peace
We can be freed from all disagreement
Others will always answer us kindly
We will no longer be tempted to anger
hard.why: He quoted Elder Soares: “We can become instruments of His peace in the world.” Peacemakers carry the Savior’s peace to others.

hard.q: Marc spoke harshly to a coworker last week. Which response best fits Elder Kyungu’s closing invitations?
options: He avoids the coworker so no more harsh words can be said
He stays silent about it and trusts time to mend the hurt
He repents of those words and now speaks to uplift and unite
He explains that he was provoked, then offers to start again
hard.why: He said, “Let us repent for the harsh language and expressions that have offended” others, and “use the language that uplifts, edifies, comforts, and brings people together.”

hard.q: In the verse Elder Kyungu quoted from Ephesians, what test does Paul give for the words we speak?
options: They should be few and carefully chosen
They should win others to our view
They should please those who lead us
They should edify and bless the hearers
hard.why: Paul wrote that our words should be “good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.”

hard.q: Which person is doing the “spiritual exercise” Elder Kyungu described after pondering President Oaks’s invitation?
options: One who avoids any conversation in which people might disagree
One who waits for others to soften their words before changing her own
One who spots a phrase of hers that stirs conflict and swaps it for words of peace
One who decides to say less everywhere so that nothing she says can offend
hard.why: He called it “a spiritual exercise to identify the language and expressions we need to forgo and then replace them with words and phrases that bring peace.” It is replacing, not just avoiding or waiting.
